topic: Day 1 · DKA Management II — Insulin & Ketone Clearance
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Diabetes & Endocrine Unit
speakerBio: A diabetologist who runs the inpatient DKA service and has seen every rebound relapse there is, all of them from stopping insulin too soon. His teaching line: you switch off the drip when the acid is gone, not when the sugar looks nice.
lectureHTML:
🎯 Where we start — 06:30, resus bay 2, two hours in

The 19-year-old is now resuscitated: two litres of saline in, systolic back to 108, glucose down from 31 to 17. Her potassium is 4.2 and she is passing urine. The fixed-rate insulin infusion is running. But her BHB is still 5.9 and her pH is 7.10 — the acid is still there. This session is about the drug that actually cures DKA: insulin — not to chase the sugar, but to switch off the ketone factory — and about the single commonest way trainees turn a recovering DKA into a relapse: stopping the insulin too soon.

1 · The one sentence that holds the session

The insulin infusion in DKA treats the ketosis, not the glucose. You run it, unchanged, until the acid is gone — and you never turn off the patient's background basal insulin while you do.

2 · The fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion (FRIII) 💉

Modern JBDS practice is a fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion (FRIII): soluble human insulin (e.g. Actrapid) at 0.1 units/kg/hour — for a 70 kg adult, 7 units/hour. "Fixed-rate" means you do not titrate it up and down against the glucose; you run a steady, physiologically effective dose that reliably switches off lipolysis and ketogenesis and clears the acid.

  • Weight-based: 0.1 units/kg/h. Use estimated weight; consider capping around 15 units/h in the very obese unless directed otherwise.
  • No routine bolus: current JBDS practice does not require a stat IV insulin bolus if the FRIII is started promptly.
  • Made up as: 50 units soluble insulin in 50 mL 0.9% saline (1 unit/mL) via syringe pump.
💡 Pearl — insulin is the ketone drug, fluid is the glucose drug

Reframe the roles and DKA becomes clear: fluid does most of the early glucose-lowering (Session 3), while insulin's unique job is to shut off ketogenesis and reverse the acidosis by restraining lipolysis and switching the liver back to storage mode. That is why the infusion is fixed and continues even after the glucose normalises (with added dextrose) — because the endpoint is clearance of ketones, not a glucose target.

3 · Keep the basal insulin running — do NOT stop it 🛡️

One of the most important and most-missed instructions in DKA: if the patient normally takes a long-acting/basal insulin (e.g. glargine/Lantus, degludec/Tresiba, detemir/Levemir), continue it at the usual dose and time throughout, running alongside the FRIII.

  • It maintains a background of basal insulinisation, so that when the intravenous infusion is eventually stopped there is no sudden insulin gap.
  • It is the key protection against rebound hyperglycaemia and rebound ketoacidosis at the point of transition off the drip.
Stop the short-acting infusion when the DKA resolves — but never stop the long-acting basal. The basal is the safety net under the trapeze.
⚠️ Danger — stopping basal insulin "because they're on a drip"

A frequent, dangerous error is withholding the patient's usual long-acting insulin during the DKA because "they're already getting insulin through the pump." The moment the FRIII is stopped there is then no insulin in the body at all — and the ketogenic machine of Session 1 restarts within an hour or two, tipping the patient straight back into DKA. Always continue the basal.

4 · Targets — is the insulin actually working? 🎯

Because insulin is fixed-rate, you monitor response and troubleshoot if targets are not met. Check hourly capillary glucose and ketones, and venous gas at intervals. The JBDS targets:

ParameterTarget rate of change
Blood ketones (BHB)Fall by ≥0.5 mmol/L per hour
Venous bicarbonateRise by ≥3 mmol/L per hour
Blood glucoseFall by ≥3 mmol/L per hour

If these targets are not being met, the response is not to stop insulin — it is to increase the FRIII (e.g. by 1 unit/h) and to check the obvious remediable causes: is the infusion actually connected and running, is the pump working, is the cannula patent, and are the fluids adequate? An insulin infusion that appears ineffective is usually a delivery failure, not insulin resistance.

🎯 Fixed-rate vs the old sliding scale

DKA is deliberately treated with a FIXED-rate infusion, not a variable-rate ("sliding-scale") insulin titrated against glucose. Why? A sliding scale titrated to glucose would wind the insulin down as the glucose fell — but the ketones would not yet be cleared, so ketogenesis would smoulder on. The fixed rate guarantees a steady, ketone-clearing dose regardless of the glucose, and we protect against hypoglycaemia by adding 10% dextrose rather than by cutting the insulin. Variable-rate infusions have their place (e.g. perioperative glycaemic control, or after DKA resolves), but the acute treatment of DKA is fixed-rate.

5 · Add 10% dextrose once glucose <14 — keep the engine running 🍬

As introduced in Session 3: once the blood glucose falls below 14 mmol/L (~250 mg/dL), start 10% dextrose (e.g. 125 mL/h) alongside the ongoing saline, and continue the FRIII unchanged. The glucose almost always normalises before the ketones do; dextrose is what lets you keep the insulin — and therefore the ketone-clearance — running without causing hypoglycaemia. If the glucose falls despite dextrose, add more dextrose (or increase its concentration) rather than reducing the insulin below the rate needed to clear ketones.

6 · Criteria for DKA resolution ✅

DKA is resolved — and only then may you plan to stop the FRIII — when all of the following are met:

CriterionThreshold
Blood ketones (BHB)<0.6 mmol/L
Venous pH>7.3
Venous bicarbonate>15 mmol/L

Note what is not on the list: the glucose. Resolution is defined by the ketones and the acid-base status, not by the blood sugar — because DKA was never a glucose disease. A patient can have a perfectly normal glucose and still be in DKA if the ketones and acidosis persist; do not stop the infusion until the acid is truly gone.

💡 Pearl — resolution is measured in ketones, not sugar

Ask three questions before stopping the drip: Is the BHB below 0.6? Is the pH above 7.3? Is the bicarbonate above 15? If any answer is no, the DKA is not resolved — keep the fixed-rate infusion running (with dextrose to hold the glucose up). The glucose being normal is necessary for comfort but is not the endpoint.

7 · Safe transition to subcutaneous insulin 🔁

Getting off the infusion safely is where DKAs relapse if done carelessly. The rules:

  • Only transition once DKA has resolved (BHB <0.6, pH >7.3, bicarbonate >15) and the patient is eating and drinking.
  • Give the subcutaneous short-acting insulin with a meal, and — critically — continue the intravenous infusion for a period of overlap (about 30–60 minutes after the subcutaneous dose) before stopping it. Short-acting subcutaneous insulin takes time to be absorbed and act; stop the drip the instant you inject and there is an insulin-free gap during which ketogenesis can restart.
  • Continue the basal insulin throughout (it was never stopped) — or, if the patient is newly diagnosed, start a basal insulin before stopping the infusion, guided by the diabetes team.
  • Ideally time the switch to a mealtime during the day, not the middle of the night, and involve the diabetes specialist team.
Overlap, don't gap. Give the subcutaneous short-acting insulin with a meal and let the infusion run 30–60 minutes into it — never inject and immediately switch off.
☠️ M&M — "The DKA had resolved, so we stopped the drip"

A 20-year-old man with type 1 diabetes recovered well from DKA overnight: by 05:00 his BHB was 0.4, pH 7.34, bicarbonate 18, glucose 9. The night team, pleased, stopped the insulin infusion immediately — and, because he had been 'on insulin all night', had also withheld his usual evening Lantus the night before and did not give any subcutaneous insulin at the point of stopping. He was not yet eating. By 09:00 he was vomiting again; a repeat gas showed pH 7.18, BHB 4.1 — a full rebound DKA. The cascade was entirely mechanistic: with the infusion off, the withheld basal, and no subcutaneous cover, he had no insulin in his body at all, and the ketogenic machine restarted within hours. Lessons: (1) never withhold the usual long-acting basal insulin during DKA; (2) do not stop the infusion until the patient is eating and has had subcutaneous short-acting insulin with a meal; (3) overlap the infusion 30–60 minutes past the subcutaneous dose. Stopping insulin a few minutes too early undid a whole night's work.

8 · Beyond the core — do not forget these 🧩

  • Find and treat the precipitant: infection, myocardial infarction, missed insulin, new diagnosis, drugs (steroids, SGLT2 inhibitors). DKA is always provoked by something.
  • VTE prophylaxis: DKA is prothrombotic (dehydration, hyperosmolality) — give thromboprophylaxis unless contraindicated (even more important in HHS).
  • Bicarbonate is almost never given: routine IV sodium bicarbonate is not recommended — correcting insulin deficiency clears the ketoacids and the pH follows; bicarbonate risks paradoxical CNS acidosis, hypokalaemia and delayed ketone clearance. Reserve for extreme, refractory acidaemia under specialist guidance.
  • Monitor potassium relentlessly (Sessions 1–3) — it is the electrolyte that kills during treatment.
  • Involve the diabetes specialist team for every DKA, and especially for transition and for new diagnoses.

9 · Take-home 🎯

  • FRIII at 0.1 units/kg/h — fixed-rate, treating the ketosis, not the glucose.
  • Continue the patient's usual long-acting basal insulin throughout — it prevents rebound DKA at transition.
  • Targets: ketones fall ≥0.5 mmol/L/h, bicarbonate rise ≥3 mmol/L/h, glucose fall ≥3 mmol/L/h. Not met → increase insulin and check delivery, don't stop it.
  • Add 10% dextrose once glucose <14 mmol/L to keep the insulin running for ketone clearance.
  • Resolution = BHB <0.6, pH >7.3, bicarbonate >15 — defined by ketones and acid, not sugar.
  • Transition safely: only when resolved and eating; give SC short-acting with a meal and overlap the infusion 30–60 min; keep the basal going.
  • Fixed-rate, not sliding-scale, in acute DKA. Find the precipitant; give VTE prophylaxis; avoid routine bicarbonate.

That closes the loop from Session 1's broken switch to a patient safely off the drip: understand the mechanism, diagnose the triad, refill the tank, and run the insulin until the acid — not the sugar — is gone.

moderatorQs.q: Why is DKA treated with a fixed-rate insulin infusion rather than a variable-rate sliding scale titrated against the glucose?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because the therapeutic target in DKA is clearance of the ketoacidosis, not control of the glucose, and the two diverge during treatment. A fixed-rate infusion (0.1 units/kg/h) guarantees a steady, physiologically effective insulin level that reliably suppresses lipolysis and ketogenesis and reverses the acidosis. A sliding scale titrated to glucose would do the wrong thing: as the glucose fell (largely from fluids), the scale would wind the insulin down while the ketones were still present, so ketogenesis would smoulder on and resolution would stall. We instead keep the insulin fixed and protect against hypoglycaemia by adding 10% dextrose once glucose falls below 14 mmol/L. Variable-rate infusions are appropriate elsewhere (perioperative control, or after DKA has resolved), but the acute treatment of DKA is deliberately fixed-rate so the ketone-clearing dose is never prematurely reduced.

moderatorQs.q: A patient's DKA has resolved biochemically at 4am. Under what conditions may you stop the insulin infusion, and how do you avoid a rebound?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: First, confirm DKA has truly resolved — BHB <0.6 mmol/L, pH >7.3, and bicarbonate >15 (resolution is defined by ketones and acid-base, not the glucose). But biochemical resolution alone is not enough to stop safely: the patient must also be eating and drinking, and you must bridge the transition to subcutaneous insulin without an insulin-free gap. Give the subcutaneous short-acting insulin with a meal and continue the intravenous infusion for an overlap of about 30–60 minutes afterwards before stopping it, because subcutaneous insulin takes time to absorb and act. Crucially, the patient's usual long-acting basal insulin should have been continued throughout and continues now. Practically, avoid switching in the middle of the night when the patient is not eating — wait for a daytime meal and involve the diabetes team. Stop the drip the moment you inject, or with the basal withheld, and you create an insulin-free window in which ketogenesis restarts — a rebound DKA.

moderatorQs.q: Two hours into treatment the ketones have barely moved — BHB has fallen only 0.1 mmol/L/h. What is your response, and what is it definitely NOT?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The target is a fall in BHB of at least 0.5 mmol/L per hour (or a bicarbonate rise ≥3 mmol/L/h and glucose fall ≥3 mmol/L/h); a fall of only 0.1 means the DKA is not resolving fast enough. The correct response is to increase the fixed-rate insulin infusion (e.g. by 1 unit/hour) and to check every remediable cause of apparent insulin failure: is the infusion actually connected and running, is the syringe pump working and programmed correctly, is the cannula patent and not tissued, was the insulin drawn up correctly, and are the fluids keeping up? An infusion that looks ineffective is far more often a delivery failure than true resistance. What it is emphatically not is a reason to stop or reduce the insulin — doing so would abandon the one drug clearing the acid. So: escalate the rate, hunt the delivery fault, ensure adequate fluid — never switch the insulin off.

audienceQs.q: The patient is on a fixed-rate insulin infusion, so why do I also need to give their normal once-daily Lantus? Isn't that doubling up on insulin?
audienceQs.answerHTML: It feels like doubling up, but it is a deliberate safety measure and you should continue the usual long-acting basal insulin (Lantus/glargine, Tresiba/degludec, Levemir/detemir) at its normal dose and time throughout the DKA. The two do different jobs: the fixed-rate infusion is the acute, ketone-clearing workhorse, while the basal maintains a steady background of insulinisation so that the moment you eventually switch the infusion off, there is no sudden insulin gap. If you had withheld the basal, then when the drip stops the patient has no insulin at all in their body, and ketogenesis — and a full rebound DKA — restarts within an hour or two. The small overlap while both run is safe and monitored (with dextrose to protect the glucose); the gap created by stopping basal is what actually harms patients. So keep the basal going: it is the safety net under the whole treatment.

audienceQs.q: The patient's glucose has come down to 11 but the ketones are still 4 and the pH is 7.15. Do I turn the insulin down to stop the glucose dropping further?
audienceQs.answerHTML: No — do not turn the insulin down. The DKA is not resolved: the ketones (4 mmol/L) and acidosis (pH 7.15) are still driving the illness, and the insulin is the drug clearing them. The glucose normalising ahead of the ketones is expected — glucose is largely corrected by fluids while the ketones take longer. The correct move is to keep the fixed-rate infusion running unchanged and add 10% dextrose (e.g. 125 mL/h) because the glucose is below 14 mmol/L, which lets you maintain the ketone-clearing insulin dose without causing hypoglycaemia. If the glucose still drifts low despite dextrose, increase the dextrose (rate or concentration) rather than cutting the insulin below the rate needed to clear ketones. You stop or reduce the insulin only once resolution criteria are met — BHB <0.6, pH >7.3, bicarbonate >15 — not because the sugar looks good.

audienceQs.q: A junior asked me to prepare IV sodium bicarbonate for a DKA patient with a pH of 7.05. Is that appropriate?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Almost certainly not, and it is right to pause. Routine intravenous sodium bicarbonate is not recommended in DKA, even at a pH of 7.05. The acidosis is caused by ketoacids, and the definitive treatment is insulin plus fluids: as insulin switches off ketogenesis, the ketoacids are metabolised, bicarbonate is regenerated, and the pH corrects itself. Giving bicarbonate carries real harms — it can cause a paradoxical worsening of intracellular/CNS acidosis, worsen hypokalaemia (dangerous when insulin is already driving potassium into cells), cause a rebound alkalosis, and delay ketone clearance. It is reserved only for extreme, life-threatening refractory acidaemia (typically pH well below 7.0 with haemodynamic instability) and then only on senior/critical-care direction. So confirm with the senior before preparing it; the far more important interventions here are ensuring the fixed-rate insulin and fluids are running and the potassium is being replaced.
